extracted.intended_audience: students and readers approaching the deeper study of Greek thought and classical poetry/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical reading and exposition of ancient Greek tragedy and myth (e.g., Euripides' Bacchae; the Homeric Hymn to Demeter), extracting their artistic devices, phases of development, and symbolic meanings. Useful for essays, lectures, or interpretive criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relieving grotesque by homely pathos and natural beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Relieve and justify what seems tedious, constrained, or merely terrible and grotesque by a suddenly suggested trait of homely pathos, or a glimpse of natural beauty, or a morsel of form or colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euripides' tactic: in a fantastic or grotesque scene shift tone by the chorus' singing or by a brief pictorial image (e.g., the fawn escaping the hunter, the 'dark-haired tresses of the wood', 'the breath of the river-side') so the audience's feelings are altered and the scene gains humane justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disguise/costume to heighten tragic irony and ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ disguise (e.g., male character in female attire) to make the protagonist ridiculous while simultaneously tightening the circle of his madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pentheus' female dress produces laughable readjustments and outward ridiculousness, yet it is also the garment of his doom—costume serves both comic effect and tragic irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing comic laughter with underlying shudder/tragic irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Create situations where immediate laughter coexists with or gives way to a deeper, more horrifying realization—audience laughter that 'will pass round the theatre' while more discerning viewers 'shudder' at the victim's fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pentheus' clumsy madness provokes laughter, but knowledge of his impending doom turns the same elements into chilling irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed coarse horror tempered by pathetic touches and landscape loveliness
rubrics_metrics.description: When depicting violent or revolting acts, balance coarse, revolting detail with pathetic (moving) touches and reminders of natural beauty or the loveliness of scenes/characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messenger narratives of Pentheus' tearing are 'full of wild, coarse, revolting details, of course not without pathetic touches, and with the loveliness of the serving Maenads, and of their mountain solitudes—their trees and water—never quite forgotten.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic psychological detail to portray incipient madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce subtle psychological symptoms that make madness feel realistic (e.g., distorted perception of weight or doubling of the sun) to deepen character portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euripides includes touches like a symptom 'in which the patient, losing the sense of resistance ... imagines himself to be raising enormous weights'—Pentheus fancies he could lift Cithaeron when he lifts a thyrsus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the chorus as tonal and structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the chorus shift tone, provide diversion, and mediate between staid civic order and wild cultic forces; the chorus can be the 'paler sisters' of the Bacchanals and also absorb the Bacchanals into itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chorus' singing diverts attention to natural images; dramaturgically the chorus legitimizes or comments on actions and can be augmented by onstage devotees to complete the conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messenger narration for gruesome actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report extreme violence through a messenger's narrative—rich in coarse detail but capable of pathos—rather than staging every grotesque act visibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pentheus' death is given in a messenger's narrative filled with 'wild, coarse, revolting details' which allows balance between horror and other aesthetic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transference/substitution of emotional weight to central deity
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fuller conception, transfer much of the horror and sorrow of mortal victims to the god figure (e.g., Dionysus) so the deity embodies both hunter and hunted aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To 'realise in the older, profounder, and more complete sense' of Dionysus, the sorrow of Agave and others must be transferred to him; this substitution deepens the tragic/aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophism/rationalist temper to soften myth's tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a rationalist explanatory device (a 'sophism') to soften older, more horrifying traditions, making them more palatable to the audience while still retaining deeper motifs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euripides' explanation that the women's violence is madness sent as punishment is a 'sophism' used to temper and rationalize the older, more savage tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing: haste and close-packing to relieve extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: Compress and hurry events in the closing stages to prevent over-dwelling on extravagant detail and to concentrate emotional impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that 'haste and close-packing of the matter' may relieve the extravagance of events and keep the mind from dwelling overmuch on horrid details, aiding pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of pathos: few profoundly designed touches
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieve deep pathos with a small number of well-chosen, powerful details (e.g., Cadmus' perplexity, Agave's gradual return to reason) rather than prolix description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euripides depicts the house's ruin and Agave's awakening by concentrated touches that render the final sorrow 'genuine, heartfelt, and dignified.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on total impression rather than minute debate
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting mythic material for imaginative/studious audiences, select and weave details to produce a total impression rather than getting bogged in disputable particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay describes itself as 'an attempt to select and weave together ... with a view rather to a total impression than to the debate of particular points.' This is guidance for exposition and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase developmental framework for myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand myth development via three phases: (1) a half-conscious/instinctive or mystical phase (oral, variable), (2) a conscious poetical/literary phase (poets fix and shape the legend), and (3) an ethical phase (persons become abstract symbols representing moral/spiritual conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to Demeter/Persephone: first primitive impressions about natural cycles; then literary fixation (Homeric hymn); finally ethical/symbolic reinterpretation in art and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personification/symbol to express natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Personify earth, growth, death, and seasons through mythic figures (e.g., Demeter as earth, Kore/Persephone as life and death) to embody complex natural processes in emotionally resonant human terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues Demeter and Persephone together represent the earth's annual changes, growth and decay, and moral or spiritual meanings associated with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess authenticity and antiquity via stylistic echoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the antiquity/authenticity of a poetic text by its stylistic features and echoes of older works (e.g., Homeric style in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter), while noting possible later additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter is treated as central and possibly pre-600 BCE; 'portions of the text are missing, and there are probably some additions by later hands'—yet scholars see genuine Homeric characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism's temper: literal metaphors and era-specific modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that intense symbolism (taking metaphors 'au pied de la lettre') arises from a special temper of age and can produce powerfully poetic imagery, though it may feel conventional to modern tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to Giotto and Blake show how earlier ages' literal or strong symbolism made figurative personifications appear genuinely alive rather than mere allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic handling of mythic networks and overlapping gods
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid isolating single elements; treat myths as overlapping networks where gods and images interpenetrate—analysis should be mindful that threads cannot always be examined in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that 'The gods of Greek mythology overlap each other ... it is only in a limited sense that it is possible to lift, and examine by itself, one thread of the network of story and imagery.'
